ground_truth.description: asyncio.wait_for raises asyncio.TimeoutError, which is only an alias of the builtin TimeoutError on Python 3.11+. On Python 3.10 and earlier they are distinct classes, so `except TimeoutError` would fail to catch the timeout and the intended legible pytest.fail diagnostic (the entire point of task 988) would never run — the raw asyncio.TimeoutError would propagate instead. Catch asyncio.TimeoutError to be version-safe.

Doubling the latency assertion bound from 2.0s to 4.0s weakens the regression guard; a real 2-3x per-call slowdown would now pass silently. Acceptable as CI-jitter mitigation but reduces the test's sensitivity.

task.title: Surface legible per-project diagnostic when two_projects_do_not_serialise rendezvous times out
task.description:
In `test_two_projects_do_not_serialise` (test_task_interceptor.py:2558-2567), the two-Event rendezvous replaces a flaky 50-tick sleep loop with a deterministic barrier. However, if a future regression drops one project's ticket before it reaches `add_task`, the surviving project hangs until the 10s `asyncio.wait_for` fires and raises `TimeoutError` with an asyncio traceback rather than a clear 'only one project entered add_task' message.

Wrap each wait in `try/except asyncio.TimeoutError` and `pytest.fail(...)` with the entered-flag state, e.g.:

```python
try:
    await asyncio.wait_for(projB_entered.wait(), timeout=10.0)
except asyncio.TimeoutError:
    pytest.fail(
        f"project A entered but B never did — "
        f"projA_entered={projA_entered.is_set()} projB_entered={projB_entered.is_set()}"
    )
```

so a regression produces a legible per-project failure message rather than an opaque timeout traceback.

Location: fused-memory/tests/test_task_interceptor.py:2558-2567
